summary: ROLIE is a resource-oriented approach for publishing, discovering and sharing security automation information. Producers can exchange software descriptors, security incidents, attack indicators, vulnerabilities and configuration checklists in a uniform way, building on web-style interfaces.

plainLanguage.summary: It is like a shared library where security teams put up and look for information about threats and weaknesses using familiar web addresses.

subtitle: A web-style way to publish, find and share security automation data, built on the Atom feed formats.

tldr.problem: Security tools need machine-readable data such as vulnerabilities, incidents and configuration checklists, but there is no uniform, discoverable way to publish and fetch it.
tldr.mechanism: ROLIE puts security resources behind web addresses and organizes them as Atom Feeds and Entries, using AtomPub Service Documents for discovery and categories to say what kind of information each Feed holds.
tldr.outcome: Producers and consumers can share many kinds of security information over HTTP with TLS and access control, and new information types can be added through IANA registries.

today: RFC 8322 is a Proposed Standard and the metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The RFC itself leaves specific information types to separate extension documents.

sections.title: What ROLIE Is
sections.content:
ROLIE (Resource-Oriented Lightweight Information Exchange) is a resource-oriented approach to sharing security automation information. It follows the REST architectural style. Security resources live in web-accessible repositories structured as Atom Syndication Format Feeds (RFC 4287).

The goal is more communication and sharing of security information between providers and consumers, so that both human operators and computer systems can automate security processes such as incident reports, vulnerability assessments and configuration checklists. Granular authentication and access controls decide who may read or write a given Feed.

Sections 5 and 6 of the RFC define the requirements for XML representations. Other equivalent representations, such as JSON, may be described by other documents.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine a notice board with a separate folder for each kind of safety news. ROLIE says how to label the folders so computers can find the right news on their own.

sections.title: Background and Motivation
sections.content:
To automate security processes, tools need structured security information. Vulnerabilities, configurations, software identification, security incidents and patch data are some of the classes already shared. As networks grow and the volume of data makes humans-in-the-loop hard to scale, machine-to-machine communication becomes more critical.

The RFC lists four benefits ROLIE aims to provide:

  • Extensible information types and format agnosticism: Entries declare the format of the data they point to, and link relations can show alternate formats such as XML or JSON.
  • Open and distributed sharing: Feeds can aggregate other Feeds and accept posted information, so webs of ROLIE servers can form ad hoc sharing communities, or a large repository can act as a central or federated collection.
  • Stateless communication: the server keeps no client sessions and uses link relations for state transitions.
  • Discovery and navigation: clients can find and walk collections to discover new or revised content.

All normative requirements in AtomPub and Atom Syndication are inherited. ROLIE may upgrade a requirement (a SHOULD to a MUST) but never downgrades one.
sections.plainLanguage: Computers cannot read a pile of loose notes, so ROLIE gives every note a label and a place. Anyone allowed in can look things up and see what is new.

sections.title: Service Documents, Collections and Feeds
sections.content:
ROLIE builds on the Atom Publishing Protocol (AtomPub, RFC 5023). A Service Document is the head of a repository. It holds one or more app:workspace elements, each holding app:collection elements. A Collection points to an Atom Feed through its href attribute. The RFC suggests grouping Collections into workspaces by the access a client needs.

A Collection or Feed counts as a ROLIE one when it carries exactly one atom:category with the scheme urn:ietf:params:rolie:category:information-type and a suitable term. That ties it to one type of security automation information. Collections and Feeds without this category are non-ROLIE and can sit alongside them in the same AtomPub instance. Additional categories with other schemes are allowed.

A ROLIE Feed MUST contain one or more atom:link elements with rel='service' pointing to its Service Document. Feeds SHOULD carry paging links (first, last, previous, next) based on RFC 5005, because new and updated Entries are ordered at the start of a Feed. The atom:updated element MUST hold the time the Feed last changed. The RFC does not give a fully automated way to find the Service Document URL.
sections.plainLanguage: The Service Document is the front-door map of the library. It lists the shelves, and each shelf holds one kind of item, with arrows to the next and previous page.

sections.title: Entries, Formats and Properties
sections.content:
Each atom:entry in a Feed describes one record, such as a specific checklist or vulnerability record. ROLIE restricts atom:content to the out-of-line form and makes it REQUIRED: exactly one per Entry, with a type naming the serialization (for example application/xml or application/json) and a src URI that can be dereferenced to fetch the data.

When no specific media type exists, the rolie:format element describes the data model. Its ns attribute is REQUIRED, must be an absolute URI, and need not be resolvable. Optional attributes are version, schema-location and schema-type. The RFC's example uses it to say the content is IODEF v2.

For metadata with unbounded values, ROLIE adds rolie:property, a name/value pair where name is a URI. An Entry may have zero or more. Clients that meet an unregistered property name MUST ignore it rather than fail parsing.

If an Entry is shared on its own, outside its Feed, it MUST carry an atom:link with rel='collection' for each containing Feed, and it MUST declare the information type of its content.
sections.plainLanguage: Each Entry is a card in the catalog. It says where the real item is kept and what language it is written in, so you can skip ones you cannot read.

sections.title: Extension Points
sections.content:
ROLIE itself does not define any information types. It expects other specifications to register them. The RFC offers a few notional examples: indicator, incident, vulnerability reports, configuration checklists and software tags.

There are four extension points:

  • Category: new information type terms, registered with IANA, become the main feature that characterizes a Collection, Feed or Entry. A category with an unregistered scheme is Private Use and must be parsed without error, though it may be ignored.
  • Format: extensions may restrict which data models are allowed for an information type. Declaring the model lets a consumer skip content it cannot use.
  • Link relations: new ones can be registered, or an absolute URI can be used if a relation is too specific.
  • Property: extensions can register named properties. Names with the prefix urn:ietf:params:rolie:property:local are Private Use.

The RFC also registers four general properties: content-author-name, content-id, content-published-date and content-updated-date. The two date properties MUST be formatted as in RFC 3339.
sections.plainLanguage: The library lets new kinds of shelves be added later. Each new shelf has to be registered so everyone agrees on its name.

sections.title: Transport and Access Control
sections.content:
ROLIE is meant to run over Transport Layer Security. Servers MUST support TLS 1.2 and SHOULD follow RFC 7525. The newest TLS version is RECOMMENDED, and if that is TLS 1.3 the RFC suggests not using 0-RTT, to prevent replay attacks. A replayed PUT, POST or DELETE could, for example, revert a frequently updated resource to an old version without the client noticing. The server MUST implement certificate-based client authentication, which may be enabled per workspace.

Implementations MUST support user authentication, though it may be disabled per Feed or workspace. Authorization mechanisms are not mandated, but implementers SHOULD check authorization for every resource access.

The security section adds guidance. Primitive schemes like HTTP Basic are rarely appropriate for sensitive information, and communities handling sensitive indicators and incidents should adopt stronger approaches such as risk-based or multi-factor authentication. Consortiums may use federated identity, with care to secure the identity provider. Authorization is the responsibility of the source system. A discovery mechanism should provide a way to authenticate the server.
sections.plainLanguage: Only people with the right pass should get into the library, and the doors are locked with a secret handshake. The RFC says to use strong passes for the sensitive shelves.

sections.title: Privacy Considerations
sections.content:
The optional author field can expose a person's identity if filled in without consent, especially in a public Feed. Implementers should take care when aggregating Entries or generating them from other data sources.

Attackers who watch POSTed Entries may correlate request time with the generated updated value to profile a user. The RFC suggests backend control of Feeds instead of HTTP POST when profiling is a risk.

Easier sharing also makes it easier to correlate data across unrelated providers. A client might assemble a data set that neither provider would have allowed alone, an undetected separation of duties violation. The RFC says this risk is not unique to ROLIE and is best mitigated by vetting clients when accounts are provisioned.
sections.plainLanguage: Putting your name on a card means everyone can see it. Also, someone who reads many libraries could piece together secrets no single library meant to give away.

sections.title: IANA Registries
sections.content:
The RFC registers the ROLIE XML namespace and schema (rolie-1.0), adds the rolie entry to the IETF URN sub-namespace registry, and creates the "ROLIE URN Parameters" registry. Registration there uses Specification Required, and requests go to the MILE Working Group list and IANA. Each name has the form {type}:{label}, where type is category or property.

A second registry, "ROLIE Information Types", records a name, an IANA-assigned index starting at 1, and reference URIs. Its policy is also Specification Required. The RFC registers no information types itself.
sections.plainLanguage: There is an official sign-up book for new shelf names and card fields, so two groups never pick the same name for different things.
